https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/20/navr.text: Menü Kereső Havasi Bertalan reagált Navracsicsék kezdeményezésére: Az egyenes út a Fidesz, a párbeszéd Magyar Péterrel lehetetlen Belföld Bánáti Anna Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Reagált Havasi Bertalan, a Fidesz kommunikációs igazgatója az MTI-nek Navracsics Tibor korábbi közigazgatási és területfejlesztési miniszter augusztus 20-i bejelentésére, miszerint párbeszédet kezdeményezne Magyarország múltjáról és jövőjéről. Havasi a bejelentést úgy kommentálta, neki az egyenes út a Fidesz, a párbeszéd Magyar Péterrel lehetetlen. A csütörtök reggel közzétett videóban Navracsics arról beszélt, hogy „két oldal helyett egyenes út kell”, mert Magyarország eljutott abba a helyzetbe, amikor „két oldal végletes, végzetes szembenállása az ország egységét rombolja, cselekvőképességét rontja”. Szerinte ezért párbeszédre van szükség, ami felülírja a két oldal szembenállását. Ígérete szerint párthovatartozástól függetlenül mindenkit hív, hogy beszélgessen az ország jövőjéről és az elmúlt 100 nap, 16 és 36 év tanulságairól. A videóban feltűnt Ferencz Orsolya egykori űrbiztos, a Fidesz volt országgyűlési képviselője is. Hogy Navracsics pontosan milyen platformon képzeli el a párbeszédet, a bejelentésből nem derült ki, mint ahogy az sem, pontosan kikkel képzeli el az „egyenes út” építését. Havasi az MTI-nek azt mondta, a Fidesznek nincs álláspontja a kezdeményezésről, de neki van, mégpedig az, hogy polgári demokrataként neki az egyenes út a Fidesz. „A Tiszával való végletes szembenállás szükséges és erősítendő. Párbeszéd Magyar Péterrel lehetetlen.” Arra a kérdésre, hogy Navracsics jelezte-e előre a pártban a kezdeményezését, Havasi azt felelte, nem tudja, de neki biztosan nem szólt a volt miniszter. Havasi szerint a Fidesz elnöksége és frakciója által júliusban elfogadott „ellenállási nyilatkozat” továbbra is érvényes . A július 21-i nyilatkozat álláspontja szerint az Alaptörvény 17. módosítása után Magyarország többé nem demokratikus jogállam. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Andy Burnham with the housing secretary, Angela Rayner. Only about 60% of homes built outside London under the Affordable Homes Programme will now be social rented houses. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham with the housing secretary, Angela Rayner. Only about 60% of homes built outside London under the Affordable Homes Programme will now be social rented houses. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images Housing Burnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homes About 40% of £10bn from Affordable Homes Programme will now go on types of housing such as sheltered and shared ownership Kiran Stacey Policy editor Mon 24 Aug 2026 17.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housing plans and boost social home building. Ministers laid out plans on Monday to spend an initial £10bn from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme on a mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy. Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing. He said when launching his campaign to become MP for Makerfield: “There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.” Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing. London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date. Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans. The Guardian view on London’s social housing: pumping billions into the economy every year | Editorial Read more The Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnham has promised will be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”. Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Growing up on a council estate and raising children as a young working mum, I know firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country. “Guardian readers will know just how important council housing is too. You will know it’s so much more than just a roof over your head – it gives working parents a safe place to raise their family, offers kids the stability needed to thrive in school and wraps a community around those who need it most.” She added: “This once-in-a-generation investment will help rewrite these stories, delivering the genuinely affordable homes our country needs, getting people off waiting lists and helping families put down roots so they can get on in life.” Ministers drop plan to relax affordable housing rules after negative response Read more Officials say that another £16bn is yet to be allocated, and that social rent homes and council houses will be prioritised in future funding rounds. Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Today’s announcement puts councils back on the pitch in the fight to end homelessness. By giving local authorities some of the funding and support they need to start delivering social homes at scale again and ramping up the percentage of funds allocated to social homes, the government has laid the foundations for its council housing revolution. “But there are still underlying obstacles which hold councils back from building. The government must use the autumn budget to finally remove these barriers, like unsustainable housing debt that councils are saddled with, to make the prime minister’s vision of a new generation of social homes a reality.” The plans contrast with those announced by Reform UK on Monday, which is promising to boost the supply of social homes by evicting foreign tenants and allowing housing associations to borrow more. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Bayeux tapestry-themed merchandise at the British Museum in London, September 2026. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters View image in fullscreen Bayeux tapestry-themed merchandise at the British Museum in London, September 2026. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters Opinion Bayeux tapestry Bayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval? Charlotte Higgins The tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artwork Sat 12 Sep 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 03.12 EDT Share I have seen the Bayeux tapestry four times since childhood, and loved it on each viewing, for the sheer miracle of its survival and the glorious vividness of its detail. But the fourth time, earlier this week, was different – how could it not be? Tapestrymania has taken hold in London. The textile has been proffered as a diplomatic symbol, the occasion for crowned heads and presidents to mingle and speechify. And, assuming you agree that it was embroidered in England by Englishwomen’s hands (since many scholars argue it was likely stitched in Canterbury rather than Bayeux, Normandy – the tapestry’s home), it is charged with the potency of return, rather than simply of arrival. If you want to see the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum , be alert for the next ticket release in October, be resigned to sitting in a long digital queue and be ready to hand over £33. Or, perhaps more realistically, be prepared for disappointment. Viewing times are restricted to protect its delicate fibres from damage, so they can’t simply be extended beyond normal hours. Demand will outstrip supply. We see celebrated artworks through the lens of our own historical moment, our own biography. Encountering the tapestry again this week, in a time of war, it seemed impossible to observe the violence of the battles it depicts without a cold dread: the decapitated trunks, the horses clashing and tumbling, the looters stripping the killed of their arms and armour. But what really struck me was how legible the artwork is. Across nearly 1,000 years, its narrative clarity is such that, in its temporary gallery, you barely need to glance up at the British Museum’s animated interpretation. All it asks of you is to look, and the story will lay itself out generously before you. The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth Read more View image in fullscreen People queueing to see the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum in London, 10 September 2026. Photograph: James Manning/PA As a child, on a school trip to Bayeux, I was encouraged to see the tapestry as a cartoon strip. That makes sense, of course, to a child, and cartoonists of recent times have often used the tapestry to riff on. In his cover for the post D-day, 15 July 1944 edition of the New Yorker, Rea Irvin lovingly parodied the tapestry, putting “George Rex” on his throne instead of Edward the Confessor and depicting landing vessels stuffed with GIs, rather than wooden ships filled with Norman troops. It was irresistible in its neat reversal: Normandy invaded from England rather than vice versa. Now, though, I’d rather see it as a visual poem. An epic of conquest. In the wake of that other recent cultural sensation, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , you do not need to be a classics nerd like me (and Mary Beard and I will make a podcast on the tapestry through a classical lens soon) to spot the resonances with ancient epic. The voyaging, the misadventures, the landing on an unfamiliar shore to be met by hostile inhabitants – and then the battle. One of the most satisfying elements of the tapestry is its pacing, which also has the feel of epic. The relatively slow buildup, with the scenes of Harold and his English setting out across the sea with falcons on their wrists, and tunics pulled up as they wade out to their boats. The drama of Harold’s capture in northern France , his retrieval by William of Normandy, and Harold’s rescue of men sinking into the quicksand at Mont Saint-Michel. The fateful (but unspecified) oath Harold swears to William. The death of Edward back in Westminster, his weeping wife and Harold’s acclamation as king of England. Finally, the clash of armies and Harold’s death. View image in fullscreen A detail of the 70m-long Bayeux tapestry, September 2026. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters But – also like an ancient epic – it has its moments of strangeness and humour. The main scenes on the textile are bordered by images of fantastic beasts, but also scenes of everyday life – of people ploughing and scattering seed. A reminder of existences that grind on despite the machinations of kings. It reminds me of how imagery works in ancient epic, where similes do a comparable job of pulling the reader out of the main action into a world of nature and ordinary people doing ordinary things. Above all, the tapestry resonates with the Aeneid , the origin myth of the Roman empire by the poet Virgil (who died in 19BC), the story of which would certainly have been available to the learned elites of 11th-century northern Europe. Like the Aeneid, the tapestry offers adventures at sea, a decisive battle, a new ruler, all heralded by the arrival of a comet signifying a great reversal. Even the feasting scene – William and his men devouring skewers of meat before the battle – has an epic feel. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion It is, then, an English epic: an origin myth for Norman power in England, a story that everyone, or nearly everyone, educated in the UK knows: 1066, Harold with an arrow in his eye, William the Conqueror. Like the Aeneid, it has surface-level propaganda stitched into it. Quite likely commissioned by William’s half-brother, Odo, in the 1070s, its business is to show viewers the inevitability of the crown’s acquisition by this new Norman king. And, since it began to be part of the British imagination from its rediscovery in the 18th century, it has been so successful at imparting that narrative that hardly anyone has heard of Edgar Ætheling , the figure who had a stronger claim on the English throne than either Harold or William, and is completely absent from the tapestry. But there is another reason for its extraordinary modern persistence than its sheer narrative force, economy and clarity. Despite its “official” status, an object created at the behest of conquering Normans, it is an incredibly open, and surprisingly even-handed, work of art. It has none of the posturing that blatant propaganda contains. Harold and William are portrayed as equals, with Harold accorded significant moments of valour and virtue – it is far from puffing up William solely as a new but better Julius Caesar who managed to conquer England, unlike Caesar, as his biographer, William of Poitiers, had it. The Latin text of the tapestry is clear but laconic. When we are told that “Harold swears an oath to William”, we are not told the nature of this oath (to support William in his claim to Edward’s crown? But who knows). The textile is an object whose story is completed by its viewer, which is why it is such a rich and generative artefact. Sometimes that “completion” has been for ill: the Nazis saw it strongly in relation to theories of racial superiority, fascinated by the Normans’ Nordic origins. And what now? The Bayeux tapestry , back (perhaps!) in England after as much as (perhaps!) 900 years, is just beginning a period of intense and excited scrutiny by a thrilled public. What will be read into those ancient threads? What will we take from it? Whatever emerges, it will almost certainly reveal more about us, now, in the 21st century, than the time in which it was made. The narrative of the tapestry is wonderfully clear. But the story it is telling us is ours to compose. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images By Joe Tidy World Service Cyber Correspondent Published 2 hours ago Cyber-criminals who hacked the FBI say they have extremely sensitive medical data for thousands of its special agents. BBC News has seen samples of the stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations, which contain information such as blood and urine test results, and doctors' notes mentioning conditions such as a "shellfish and banana allergy". The records include agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical concerns including 'blood in the urine' and 'high cholesterol'. Experts say the hack - which the FBI is investigating - could leave agents vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks, as well as help criminals impersonate law enforcement officers. "The list maps thousands of agents against their medical and fitness records," said Etay Maor, vice-president of threat intelligence at Cato Networks. "Passwords can be reset if stolen, but medical records cannot, so once this data is out, it stays compromised for good. That permanence, applied across an entire workforce, is what makes this leak so serious." The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday it acknowledged the breach and said it was "aggressively investigating" how it happened. The cyber-criminal group ShinyHunters claims it breached FBI systems on Monday, and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site. The group also shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand. Unusually, the hackers are not demanding money. Instead, they are seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May, which they claim "offended" them. The samples shared with journalists appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses. The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors. Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, has described the hack - if confirmed - "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches." 'Phishing, impersonation, identity fraud' The news agency Reuters reports that some of the data includes information on agents , external involved in investigations relating to Russia, China and drug cartels. Reporting by 404 Media suggests details of a previously little-known FBI hacking unit may also have been exposed , external . It was initially thought the breach affected the FBI's 38,000 current employees, but the hackers now claim the number could be far higher. The group says it underestimated the scale of the data theft and now claims to hold sensitive information on around 60,000 current and former FBI staff. Jamie Akhtar, chief executive and co-founder of CyberSmart, said the hackers' claims should be treated with caution but that the breach appeared to be extremely concerning. "Such data could be used for highly convincing phishing, impersonation, identity fraud, blackmail or even operations targeting law-enforcement personnel, making the potential implications particularly serious," he said. The hackers, who communicate with reporters in English via the messaging service, Telegram, say they will publish the full dataset in five days unless the FBI meets their demands. ShinyHunters is an international hacking collective that has been active since 2019 and has been linked to a number of high-profile cyber-attacks, including incidents affecting Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas . The group claims it exploited a vulnerability in an Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI, gaining access to multiple platforms including FBIJobs, FBI BEAST, which handles background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which stores medical records, and FBI BICS, which contains investigative information. In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was still trying to determine whether the hackers had breached its systems directly or compromised a third-party provider. "We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the statement said. https://www.theage.com.au/world/europe/a.text: Advertisement Kyiv, Ukraine: Australia is exposed to a deepening military alliance between Russia, China and North Korea as the three partners work together in the war on Ukraine, prompting experts to warn of security risks in Asia. Former CIA director General David Petraeus warned that China was proving its capacity to design new weaponry and manufacture it in large volumes for Russia, heightening concerns for all Western nations. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin tour an exhibition in Beijing in May. Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP Political leaders and experts also pointed to the Kremlin’s reliance on North Korea as a rising threat to Asia, given that the rogue state is supplying Russia with scores of missiles in an expanding weapons trade. Petraeus, who served for 37 years in the US Army, told this masthead that China was innovating rapidly to supply Russia and apply lessons from the war in Ukraine. Advertisement “We should be very concerned that China is learning assiduously from what Russia and Ukraine are doing,” he said on the sidelines of a security conference in Kyiv. David Petraeus was America's most high-profile general for much of the past 20 years. AP “It’s providing the bulk of the components for the Russian military-industrial complex, and it is a leader in the world in robotic systems and drones and so forth. “And it has an ability to do something that is hugely important in this war, which is not just to innovate but to scale the production of those weapons.” Petraeus, an influential voice in defence investment as chairman of the KKR Global Institute, forecast a total shift in military doctrine due to the changing nature of war in Ukraine and argued that China was a key force in the conflict. Advertisement Related Article Russia-Ukraine war The new terror stalking Kyiv day and night As the “manufacturing capital” of the world, he said, China was gaining expertise in the mass production of drones and other weapons. “We should obviously be very keenly aware of that,” he said. “We should be very keenly aware of what is being developed here on this battlefield because it is the future of war, and it’s changing quite rapidly. “And that should lead us, all Western countries, to develop a new concept of war that can drive, urgently, revolutionary institutional change.” One of the most influential investors in new drones, former Google chairman Eric Schmidt, said that he saw the impact of Russia’s partnership with North Korea during a previous visit to the Ukrainian capital. Advertisement “The North Koreans are giving the Russians the KN-25, which is a major ballistic missile – it’s an enormous size and does enormous damage,” he told this masthead. “I was here when it was shot at Kyiv. I know it to be true. That’s very, very worrisome. So the connection between China and North Korea and Russia is a great concern.” North Korean leader Kim Jong-un inspects a Hwasong-17 intercontinental ballistic missile. AP One of Schmidt’s companies, Perennial Autonomy, develops the Merops interceptor drones used by regiments across Ukraine and sold at low cost, in a sign of his support for the country. The defence and investment chiefs were at the Yalta European Strategies Conference in Kyiv in recent days, where most discussions focused on the threat to Europe posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. Advertisement Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Four years on, Ukraine is under more pressure than ever. So is Russia Rising risks to Asia region The risks for the Indo-Pacific, however, are rising as Russia relies on China and North Korea. Petraeus estimated that Russia would build 10 million drones this year, while Ukraine was seeking to increase its production from 8 million to 10 million. North Korea has supplied an estimated 10,000 troops to Russia, as well as large volumes of artillery ammunition and more than 100 missiles. Advertisement Former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt said concern should not only be about what Russia received, particularly in Asia. ‘It may seem like Ukraine’s a long way away from Australia, but the North Koreans don’t think so.’ Emily Thornberry, chair of Britain’s parliamentary foreign affairs committee “The worrying thing is, of course, that the Russians are delivering things back,” he told this masthead. Bildt noted speculation that North Korea wanted to build a nuclear submarine and needed Russian help to develop the propulsion systems. Dame Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the British parliament, said that Asia would see the impact of the ties between Russia and its partners. Advertisement “It may seem like Ukraine’s a long way away from Australia, but the North Koreans don’t think so, right? They’re sending troops in to fight for the Russians,” the Labour MP said on the sidelines of the conference. A North Korean government image shows soldiers assembled with short-range, nuclear-capable missiles. AP “I mean, it’s extraordinary, what’s going on – the idea that there’s an Asian country that’s just sending their troops through. China doesn’t seem to be doing anything about it. “China’s closeness to Russia is really interesting, and I think that Russia is essentially, in order to get the help, becoming a vassal state of China. “And that, I think, does have an impact on geopolitics and will have an impact on Australia. Advertisement “So you can’t close your eyes and look the other way and think that’s a long way away because everything is connected with everything else these days.” A Polish soldier activates a Merops in 2025. Omar Marques/Getty Images Concerns about the Kremlin’s partners in East Asia are yet to result in any consensus on the best international response, despite attempts to impose sanctions on Russia to stymie vital supplies. A draft US law proposed by Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died in early July , would toughen sanctions on Russia and give the American president the power to impose sanctions on nations that trade with it – including China. Some Democrat and Republican politicians are seeking to force the bill through Congress in a debate that could begin later this month. Advertisement Related Article Opinion North Korea diplomacy The Chinese president has arrived in North Korea. The world is watching Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Even if the bill passes, it would be up to the president to decide whether to apply 100 per cent tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India. President Donald Trump aired his frustration with Ukraine on Sunday (early on Monday AEST) in a complaint about its attacks on Russian oil refineries. “Mr Zelensky has to do one thing: he has to ‌stop ⁠knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland . “We spoke ​to Mr ⁠Zelensky about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel. That’s hurting the ​world.” American journalist and author Anne Applebaum responded on X: “How about calling on Putin to stop killing Ukrainian civilians.” Advertisement While Western nations could try to impose sanctions on China, Professor Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the cost might be too high. Loading “The minute we do it, they will retaliate, which will harm our economies,” he said. “So that’s the reason why they’re shying away, and that’s the point why, at the end of the day, you know, the Russians will be supplied with whatever they need in order to assemble their weapons.” Masala, author of the recent book If Russia Wins , said that the pressure was on Europe to increase defence production to support Ukraine and prevent a Russian victory. “The only thing is to basically outproduce China, to create the industrial base for a much stronger support for Ukraine,” he told this masthead. Advertisement Related Article War Are we in World War III, and just don’t know it? China, however, appears to feel little competition from other nations in its production of military drones and other weapons. “I think this war suits China just fine,” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the YES conference. “China is getting a vassal not just on the cheap, [but] making money in the process – taking over the Russian market for everything. “If I were a Russian nationalist I would be horrified that Russia will become a very, very junior partner to China.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
